reason: Start by building the peripheral nerve route needed to carry sensory information inward and motor signals outward.
expectation: Schwann cells will wrap the nerve fibres, likely producing a myelinated peripheral nerve.

alternatives.reason: Building the spinal cord also supports the routes, but I prefer to start at the periphery.

effect: The peripheral nerve is now myelinated, with spikes renewed at gaps; I can build the central route next.
reaction: The inset clarifies how the insulating wraps relate to spike propagation.
reason: Build the spinal cord as the next link between peripheral sensory fibres and the brain.
expectation: The grey matter and surrounding white-matter tracts will form a spinal cord model.

reaction: The cross-section makes their arrangement clear.
reason: Connect the peripheral nerve to the spinal cord to establish the route for incoming and outgoing signals.
expectation: The nerve and cord will form a connected pathway, though the exact result is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: The brain is also needed, but connecting the existing peripheral and spinal parts comes first.

effect: Sensory and motor fibres share a peripheral nerve but enter and leave different sides of the cord; local circuits connect their routes.
reaction: The cross-section makes the separation of incoming and outgoing routes clear.
reason: Build the brain to complete the central structures needed to trace sensation.
expectation: The grey and white matter will form a brain model that can connect to the spinal route.

expectation: The brain and spinal pathways will join into a connected nervous-system model.

alternatives.reason: Touch could be traced into the cord first, but connecting the brain should prepare the full route.

effect: The brain, cord and peripheral nerves now form a connected model, ready for tracing signals.
reaction: The distinction between connected pathways and a signal's particular destination is useful.
reason: Trace touch from the periphery toward the brain to address the sensory goal.
expectation: The touch signal will follow sensory pathways through the spinal cord toward the brain; the exact route is uncertain.

A cortical motor route is also needed, but I want to trace sensation first.

effect: Touch activity reaches the cortex via the cord, brainstem and thalamic relay, completing the sensory goal.
reaction: The labelled thalamus makes its relay role clear.
reason: Trace the cortical motor route to address the remaining goal.
expectation: Motor activity will travel from the cortex down toward an outgoing motor nerve, though the exact pathway is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Pain could reveal a spinal route, but I chose the cortical route.

effect: The cortical command reaches a spinal motor neuron before continuing along a peripheral axon; both chapter goals are complete.
reaction: The shared final motor neuron usefully connects the long and local routes.

mostWorthwhile.text: Tracing touch to the cortex was most worthwhile: the planned illustration connects the peripheral nerve, cord, brainstem and labelled thalamic relay.

leastWorthwhile.text: Building the spinal cord and brain was comparatively predictable; their cutaways showed their arrangement but offered little explanation beyond it.

surprise.text: The final result clarified that descending and local spinal routes can influence the same motor neurons, rather than being wholly separate outputs.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, although combining generic grey matter with brain white matter simplified a complex construction without explaining how those components form the brain.

continue.text: Yes, I would be interested in another chapter: tracing signals through connected structures was useful, though I would want more detail about how the pathways work.
